articles.title: Precio del GNV, GLP, diésel y gasolina en Perú HOY, 21 de noviembre: revisa los precios y los grifos más baratos
articles.summary: Los valores recogidos este sábado muestran diferencias importantes entre establecimientos de la capital. Conoce cómo consultar el precio del GNV, GLP, diésel y gasohol en tu distrito y reportar un cobro distinto al anunciado.
articles.body_text: Los conductores peruanos que tienen previsto abastecer sus vehículos este sábado 21 de noviembre deben prestar atención a las diferencias de precios entre las estaciones de servicio. Una revisión de las tarifas reportadas en Lima muestra que el gasohol regular se comercializa desde S/ 18,56 por galón en algunos establecimientos, mientras que el premium alcanza los S/ 27,99. El diésel y los combustibles vehiculares a gas también presentan variaciones según la ubicación del grifo. Ante este panorama, la plataforma Facilito del Organismo Supervisor de la Inversión en Energía y Minería (Osinergmin) permite comparar los montos antes de realizar una compra. El gasohol regular presenta diferencias considerables en Lima. Según los precios declarados en Facilito, Comas registra tarifas desde S/ 18,56 por galón, mientras que en Lurigancho el precio mínimo alcanza los S/ 18,79. En otros distritos, como Breña, San Juan de Lurigancho y Ancón, también se encuentran alternativas con distintos valores, dependiendo del establecimiento. En el caso del gasohol premium, la brecha es todavía mayor. Ate registra precios desde S/ 20,39 por galón, mientras que en La Molina algunos establecimientos llegan a cobrar S/ 27,99. Esta diferencia demuestra que elegir correctamente dónde abastecerse puede representar un ahorro importante, especialmente para quienes utilizan su automóvil diariamente. Los usuarios de vehículos que funcionan con diésel también deben comparar las tarifas antes de acudir a una estación de servicio. La información revisada para este sábado muestra que el diésel B5 S-50 UV registra precios desde S/ 23,89 por galón en San Juan de Lurigancho, mientras que en Ancón se reportan valores de hasta S/ 30,36. Esta diferencia puede tener un impacto considerable para los conductores de transporte público, taxis, camiones y unidades de reparto. Por ejemplo, abastecer un tanque con 15 galones puede representar una diferencia de S/ 97,05 entre los precios extremos señalados. Por ello, revisar las tarifas cercanas a la ruta habitual es una alternativa para controlar los gastos de combustible. El Gas Licuado de Petróleo (GLP) vehicular y el Gas Natural Vehicular (GNV) continúan siendo alternativas para los conductores que cuentan con vehículos adaptados para utilizar estos combustibles. En Lima, los precios registrados este 21 de noviembre muestran que el GLP vehicular tiene un promedio de S/ 9,22 por galón, con tarifas desde S/ 8,65 en algunos establecimientos. En cuanto al GNV, el precio promedio reportado en Lima alcanza los S/ 1,68 por metro cúbico, mientras que algunas estaciones presentan tarifas desde S/ 1,60. Es importante recordar que el GNV se comercializa por metro cúbico y el GLP vehicular por galón, por lo que sus valores no deben compararse directamente con los precios de la gasolina o el diésel. Los conductores pueden utilizar la plataforma oficial Facilito de Osinergmin para conocer cuánto cuesta el combustible en los establecimientos registrados. El sistema permite seleccionar el departamento, provincia y distrito, además de identificar los grifos que comercializan gasohol regular, premium, diésel, GLP y GNV. De esta manera, cada usuario puede comparar las tarifas disponibles antes de salir de casa. La herramienta también permite revisar la ubicación de las estaciones, los productos disponibles y la hora de actualización de los precios declarados. Sin embargo, los montos son referenciales y pueden cambiar durante el día. Por ello, antes de realizar el abastecimiento, es recomendable comprobar el precio exhibido en el surtidor y confirmar que el establecimiento tenga combustible disponible. Las diferencias entre los precios de los combustibles responden a diversos factores, entre ellos los costos de transporte, almacenamiento, distribución, condiciones del mercado internacional y márgenes comerciales de cada establecimiento. Por esa razón, dos grifos ubicados en una misma zona pueden ofrecer tarifas distintas para un mismo producto. A ello se suma el contexto de abastecimiento energético. El Ministerio de Energía y Minas declaró en situación de emergencia las actividades de hidrocarburos mediante la Resolución Ministerial N.° 490-2026-MINEM/DM, con una vigencia de hasta ocho meses y un enfoque preventivo frente a posibles eventos climáticos que puedan afectar la cadena de suministro. La medida busca proteger la continuidad del abastecimiento y no significa, por sí sola, que exista una escasez generalizada de combustibles en el país.

articles.body_text: El líder de Renovación Popular, Rafael López Aliaga, negó haber interrumpido el contacto con el tercer regidor electo de Lima por su partido, Jesús Gálvez, y dijo que es él quien lo mantiene bloqueado en WhatsApp. Sin embargo, justificó su pedido a Gálvez a para que renuncie a su militancia partidaria tras detectar aparentes contradicciones e irregularidades durante el reciente proceso electoral. “Para empezar, si quiere hablar, que no me bloquee (...) Le hemos enviado un mensaje ahorita y no hay manera que me responda. Le he enviado dos mensajes para hablar justamente y estoy bloqueado por él. Yo no le he bloqueado a él”, dijo este jueves al programa Beto a Saber de Willax TV. Acto siguiente, mostró su celular para mostrar que sus mensajes no eran recibidos por la otra parte. La declaración de López Aliaga respondió a las declaraciones que dio Gálvez en el programa “Siempre a las 8” de Jimmy Chinchay de El Comercio, en la que el también alcalde de Jesús María afirmó entre lágrimas haber sido apartado del partido mediante un mensaje de texto. En sus comentarios, dijo que se le pidió su renuncia sin oportunidad de dar sus descargos porque, según él, “había varios inconvenientes, hay información tergiversada que le debe haber llegado y que no hemos podido todavía aclarar”. Entre los argumentos expuestos, el dirigente enfatizó la postulación de Sergio Castromonte, excoordinador de proyectos de la Municipalidad de Jesús María bajo la gestión de Gálvez, a la alcaldía distrital de La Molina por una agrupación política rival. Según detalló López Aliaga, el candidato conocido como “el bombero” constituye un indicio de interferencia y respaldo a una candidatura que compitió de manera directa contra la postulación de Renovación Popular en dicho distrito. Un segundo cuestionamiento se relacionó con la falta de apoyo proselitista a favor del candidato distrital de Renovación Popular en Jesús María. articles.title: Sismo de magnitud 6.7 en Junín dejó un muerto, 15 heridos y más de 850 damnificados
articles.summary: El sismo de magnitud 6,7, registrado el último viernes en la región Junín, dejó como saldo un muerto, 15 heridos, más de 850 personas damnificadas y varias réplicas fuertes en las últimas 48 horas.
articles.body_text: El sismo de magnitud 6,7, registrado el último viernes en la región Junín, dejó como saldo un muerto, 15 heridos, más de 850 personas damnificadas y varias réplicas fuertes en las últimas 48 horas. Según el último reporte del Centro de Operaciones de Emergencia Nacional (COEN) del Instituto Nacional de Defensa Civil (Indeci), el fallecido es un hombre de iniciales P.C.J.L. (42), que dejó de existir en el Hospital Regional Hermilio Valdizán de Huánuco. El movimiento telúrico dejó 15 heridos en las regiones Junín y Pasco, así como 853 personas damnificadas y otras 628 afectadas en cinco departamentos del país. Los heridos presentan traumatismos superficiales múltiples y fueron atendidos en establecimientos de salud de las provincias de Chanchamayo y Pasco. Once de ellos ya recibieron el alta médica. También se reporta el colapso total de la torre de la iglesia católica del caserío de Paucalin, en el distrito de Páucar, provincia de Daniel Alcides Carrión. La estructura estaba construida con material rústico (adobe) y cayó por completo. En el distrito de Santa Ana de Tusi, provincia de Daniel Alcides Carrión, se reportaron daños estructurales en 13 viviendas de adobe, en la institución educativa inicial y en la primaria N.° 34149. Mientras tanto en la provincia de Oxapampa, en el caserío de Santa Cruz, distrito de Pozuzo, se registraron rajaduras en dos viviendas, un comedor institucional, una institución educativa, una casa comunal, el local de la Tenencia de Gobernación y un puesto de salud. Hubo tres réplicas. El primero, de magnitud 5.0 se registró en Junín, en el mismo lugar del temblor de 6.7 que sacudió la noche del viernes 20 a esa y otras regiones del país, e incluso se sintió en capitales del extranjero como Quito (Ecuador) y Bogotá (Colombia). El segundo temblor del sábado también se registró en Junín, pero con epicentro a 13 kilómetros al suroeste de Chupaca. El último, de magnitud 5, se reportó en el distrito de Junín la tarde de este domingo 22 de noviembre.

articles.title: Fuertes lluvias se registran en Piura: Chulucanas y Tambogrande las zonas más afectadas
articles.summary: Fuertes lluvias se vienen registrando este domingo 22 de noviembre en la región Piura, siendo Chulucanas y Tambogrande las zonas más afectadas por las intensas precipitaciones.
articles.body_text: Fuertes lluvias se vienen registrando este domingo 22 de noviembre en la región Piura, siendo Chulucanas y Tambogrande las zonas más afectadas por las intensas precipitaciones. Según diversos reportes de usuarios en las redes sociales, las lluvias estuvieron acompañadas de descargas eléctricas. Ante ello, las autoridades advirtieron del riesgo de activación de quebradas. El núcleo de lluvia más intenso se encuentra en los sectores de Las Lomas y Tambogrande, aproximadamente a 40 o 50 kilómetros al noroeste de Chulucanas. Las precipitaciones provocaron inundaciones en la zona. Según el especialista Abraham Levy, en las últimas horas se sumaron una tormenta entre Talara y Sullana y precipitaciones en la zona más alta del valle de Piura y Lambayeque. “Precipitaciones superan ya 100mm en la zona central de la región Piura. Todo el corredor de Las Lomas-Tambogrande-Chulucanas es el más afectado”, detalló en su cuenta en “X” (antes Twitter). Cabe indicar que según el Servicio Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología (Senamhi), la región Piura registró temperaturas de hasta 37,2 °C el último sábado 21 de noviembre. De acuerdo con los registros de la Dirección Zonal 1, la estación meteorológica de Mallares, en Sullana, reportó la temperatura más alta, con 37,2 °C, seguida de San Miguel, en Catacaos, con 37 °C; Miraflores, en Piura, con 36 °C; y Lancones, con 35 °C. Los especialistas explicaron que las elevadas temperaturas están asociadas, entre otros factores, al calentamiento anómalo de la superficie del mar frente a la costa norte, donde se han identificado anomalías térmicas positivas de hasta 7 °C respecto de los valores normales.

articles.title: Piura alcanzó los 37,2 °C y ola de calor persistirá en los próximos días, advierte el Senamhi
articles.summary: El Servicio Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Perú (Senamhi) informó que la región Piura registró temperaturas de hasta 37,2 °C el último sábado 21 de noviembre y que el calor persistirá hasta el martes 24.
articles.body_text: El Servicio Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Perú (Senamhi) informó que la región Piura registró temperaturas de hasta 37,2 °C el último sábado 21 de noviembre y que el calor persistirá hasta el martes 24. Ante estas condiciones, el organismo adscrito al Ministerio del Ambiente (Minam) recomendó a la población evitar la exposición prolongada al sol, mantenerse hidratada y adoptar medidas de protección para prevenir afectaciones a la salud. De acuerdo con los registros de la Dirección Zonal 1 del SENAMHI, la estación meteorológica de Mallares, en Sullana, reportó la temperatura más alta, con 37,2 °C, seguida de San Miguel, en Catacaos, con 37 °C; Miraflores, en Piura, con 36 °C; y Lancones, con 35 °C. Los especialistas explicaron que las elevadas temperaturas están asociadas, entre otros factores, al calentamiento anómalo de la superficie del mar frente a la costa norte, donde se han identificado anomalías térmicas positivas de hasta 7 °C respecto de los valores normales. Estas condiciones favorecen un ambiente cálido y húmedo, con mayor sensación de bochorno, incluso durante las noches. Este comportamiento se encuentra contemplado en el Aviso Meteorológico Regional N.° 213, vigente del 21 al 24 de noviembre, que advierte sobre el incremento de la temperatura diurna en sectores de la costa y sierra norte, con niveles de peligro moderado, fuerte y extremo, según la zona. En Piura, las condiciones previstas comprenden sectores de las provincias de Sullana, Piura, Paita, Talara y Sechura. Ante la persistencia de las altas temperaturas, el Senamhi recomendó evitar la exposición prolongada al sol, especialmente durante las horas de mayor radiación, mantenerse hidratado y extremar las medidas de protección de niños, adultos mayores y otros grupos vulnerables al calor.

articles.title: Precio del GNV, GLP, diésel y gasolina en Perú HOY, 21 de noviembre: revisa los precios y los grifos más baratos
articles.summary: Los valores recogidos este sábado muestran diferencias importantes entre establecimientos de la capital. Conoce cómo consultar el precio del GNV, GLP, diésel y gasohol en tu distrito y reportar un cobro distinto al anunciado.
articles.body_text: Los conductores peruanos que tienen previsto abastecer sus vehículos este sábado 21 de noviembre deben prestar atención a las diferencias de precios entre las estaciones de servicio. Una revisión de las tarifas reportadas en Lima muestra que el gasohol regular se comercializa desde S/ 18,56 por galón en algunos establecimientos, mientras que el premium alcanza los S/ 27,99. El diésel y los combustibles vehiculares a gas también presentan variaciones según la ubicación del grifo. Ante este panorama, la plataforma Facilito del Organismo Supervisor de la Inversión en Energía y Minería (Osinergmin) permite comparar los montos antes de realizar una compra. El gasohol regular presenta diferencias considerables en Lima. Según los precios declarados en Facilito, Comas registra tarifas desde S/ 18,56 por galón, mientras que en Lurigancho el precio mínimo alcanza los S/ 18,79. En otros distritos, como Breña, San Juan de Lurigancho y Ancón, también se encuentran alternativas con distintos valores, dependiendo del establecimiento. En el caso del gasohol premium, la brecha es todavía mayor. Ate registra precios desde S/ 20,39 por galón, mientras que en La Molina algunos establecimientos llegan a cobrar S/ 27,99. Esta diferencia demuestra que elegir correctamente dónde abastecerse puede representar un ahorro importante, especialmente para quienes utilizan su automóvil diariamente. Los usuarios de vehículos que funcionan con diésel también deben comparar las tarifas antes de acudir a una estación de servicio. La información revisada para este sábado muestra que el diésel B5 S-50 UV registra precios desde S/ 23,89 por galón en San Juan de Lurigancho, mientras que en Ancón se reportan valores de hasta S/ 30,36. Esta diferencia puede tener un impacto considerable para los conductores de transporte público, taxis, camiones y unidades de reparto. Por ejemplo, abastecer un tanque con 15 galones puede representar una diferencia de S/ 97,05 entre los precios extremos señalados. Por ello, revisar las tarifas cercanas a la ruta habitual es una alternativa para controlar los gastos de combustible. El Gas Licuado de Petróleo (GLP) vehicular y el Gas Natural Vehicular (GNV) continúan siendo alternativas para los conductores que cuentan con vehículos adaptados para utilizar estos combustibles. En Lima, los precios registrados este 21 de noviembre muestran que el GLP vehicular tiene un promedio de S/ 9,22 por galón, con tarifas desde S/ 8,65 en algunos establecimientos. En cuanto al GNV, el precio promedio reportado en Lima alcanza los S/ 1,68 por metro cúbico, mientras que algunas estaciones presentan tarifas desde S/ 1,60. Es importante recordar que el GNV se comercializa por metro cúbico y el GLP vehicular por galón, por lo que sus valores no deben compararse directamente con los precios de la gasolina o el diésel. Los conductores pueden utilizar la plataforma oficial Facilito de Osinergmin para conocer cuánto cuesta el combustible en los establecimientos registrados. El sistema permite seleccionar el departamento, provincia y distrito, además de identificar los grifos que comercializan gasohol regular, premium, diésel, GLP y GNV. De esta manera, cada usuario puede comparar las tarifas disponibles antes de salir de casa. La herramienta también permite revisar la ubicación de las estaciones, los productos disponibles y la hora de actualización de los precios declarados. Sin embargo, los montos son referenciales y pueden cambiar durante el día. Por ello, antes de realizar el abastecimiento, es recomendable comprobar el precio exhibido en el surtidor y confirmar que el establecimiento tenga combustible disponible. Las diferencias entre los precios de los combustibles responden a diversos factores, entre ellos los costos de transporte, almacenamiento, distribución, condiciones del mercado internacional y márgenes comerciales de cada establecimiento. Por esa razón, dos grifos ubicados en una misma zona pueden ofrecer tarifas distintas para un mismo producto. A ello se suma el contexto de abastecimiento energético. El Ministerio de Energía y Minas declaró en situación de emergencia las actividades de hidrocarburos mediante la Resolución Ministerial N.° 490-2026-MINEM/DM, con una vigencia de hasta ocho meses y un enfoque preventivo frente a posibles eventos climáticos que puedan afectar la cadena de suministro. La medida busca proteger la continuidad del abastecimiento y no significa, por sí sola, que exista una escasez generalizada de combustibles en el país.

articles.body_text: El líder de Renovación Popular, Rafael López Aliaga, negó haber interrumpido el contacto con el tercer regidor electo de Lima por su partido, Jesús Gálvez, y dijo que es él quien lo mantiene bloqueado en WhatsApp. Sin embargo, justificó su pedido a Gálvez a para que renuncie a su militancia partidaria tras detectar aparentes contradicciones e irregularidades durante el reciente proceso electoral. “Para empezar, si quiere hablar, que no me bloquee (...) Le hemos enviado un mensaje ahorita y no hay manera que me responda. Le he enviado dos mensajes para hablar justamente y estoy bloqueado por él. Yo no le he bloqueado a él”, dijo este jueves al programa Beto a Saber de Willax TV. Acto siguiente, mostró su celular para mostrar que sus mensajes no eran recibidos por la otra parte. La declaración de López Aliaga respondió a las declaraciones que dio Gálvez en el programa “Siempre a las 8” de Jimmy Chinchay de El Comercio, en la que el también alcalde de Jesús María afirmó entre lágrimas haber sido apartado del partido mediante un mensaje de texto. En sus comentarios, dijo que se le pidió su renuncia sin oportunidad de dar sus descargos porque, según él, “había varios inconvenientes, hay información tergiversada que le debe haber llegado y que no hemos podido todavía aclarar”. Entre los argumentos expuestos, el dirigente enfatizó la postulación de Sergio Castromonte, excoordinador de proyectos de la Municipalidad de Jesús María bajo la gestión de Gálvez, a la alcaldía distrital de La Molina por una agrupación política rival. Según detalló López Aliaga, el candidato conocido como “el bombero” constituye un indicio de interferencia y respaldo a una candidatura que compitió de manera directa contra la postulación de Renovación Popular en dicho distrito. Un segundo cuestionamiento se relacionó con la falta de apoyo proselitista a favor del candidato distrital de Renovación Popular en Jesús María. articles.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Three significant backers share what gave them conviction to bet billions on Anthropic.
articles.body_text: When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history. But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year. “We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch. Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said. Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times. Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation. “Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials. Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch. After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said. “It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations. articles.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development | TechCrunch
articles.summary: To establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how to measure speed.
articles.body_text: A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity. Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement. In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.” Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5. “GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.” So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . articles.title: The best apps to make new friends right now | TechCrunch
articles.summary: We've compiled a list of friendship apps, from friend discovery platforms like BFF to event-focused ones like Timeleft.
articles.body_text: In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this issue a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships. Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities. According to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble’s BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025. The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations. From major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We’ve compiled a list of them for you to try out. The app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results. The app sends invitations to nearby public social events, such as wine bars and comedy clubs. There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event. A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one. The service charges a $22.22 curation fee or a monthly subscription for the same price. Dating giant Bumble is among the more established players to enter the friendship space, launching its friend-finding feature in 2016, which then spun out into a stand-alone app in 2023. The friend-making app has recently undergone a significant redesign , with an increased emphasis on facilitating group meetups, catering to users’ desires to grow their social circles. BFF is available for free download on iOS and Android devices. Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events. As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store .

articles.title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Journalist Paris Marx unpacks his new book "Hyperscale."
articles.body_text: In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine. The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections . And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power . In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.” “It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.” He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.” During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center. I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in? Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so. I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security. Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it. Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby. It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A/B testing robots vs. humans | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
articles.body_text: Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry. There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance? A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink. Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world. A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services. Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available. Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November. Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.) That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too. It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers. You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra . Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes. articles.title: Can a TV be too large? An investigation | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Can a TV be too large? This writer's recent upgrade to a 65-inch OLED came with some unexpected challenges.
articles.body_text: For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED. The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows. They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024. At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic. However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache. I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain. “I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor , who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.” Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?” There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen. Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having. In considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a big screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car. After a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison.

articles.title: A tale of two Nvidias | TechCrunch
articles.summary: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia — the company’s latest earnings report vs. the tech executives loudly calling for Jensen Huang’s return.
articles.body_text: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return. Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.) Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China. What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down. A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027. Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country. Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China. And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line. Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline. It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

articles.title: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A U.S. startup is seeking $162 million in damages and an injunction to impact iPhone and Apple Watch imports to India.
articles.body_text: Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology. GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch , an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch. Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims. In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company launched StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024. Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1. “We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing. In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale. Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android . Apple did not respond to a request for comment. India has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China . The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth. articles.title: Steven Spielberg’s Ready Player One improves immensely on the book
articles.summary: Ernest Cline’s fast-moving, bestselling novel was a treasure trove for pop-culture junkies. But the endless references to video games and movies work better on the screen, where most of them originated in the first place.
articles.body_text: Fans tend to either love or hate Ernest Cline’s bestselling 2011 novel Ready Player One. There are legitimate reasons for both reactions. On the love side: it’s a light, airy pop confection, crammed with familiar cultural references, which Cline recontextualizes in surprising ways. On the hate side: the prose can be extremely clumsy, as it is in this paragraph where teenage protagonist Wade Watts describes the virtual car he constructed for himself in the vast online world where he spends most of his waking hours: > The DeLorean came outfitted with a (nonfunctioning) flux capacitor, but I’d made several additions to its equipment and appearance. First, I’d installed an artificially intelligent onboard computer named KITT (purchased in an online auction) into the dashboard, along with a matching red Knight Rider scanner just above the DeLorean’s grill. Then I’d outfitted the car with an oscillation overthruster, a device that allowed it to travel through solid matter. Finally, to complete my ‘80s super-vehicle theme, I’d slapped a Ghostbusters logo on each of the DeLorean’s gull-wing doors, then added personalized plates that read ECTO-88. That’s a lot of awkward verbiage to say two pretty basic things: people in virtual reality can express their personal tastes through their avatars in hyper-specific ways, and Cline is so obsessed with the culture of the 1980s — the geek-fodder of his youth — that he thinks it’s compelling even in the form of a shopping list. The book is a fast-paced adventure, but this kind of unwieldy lump of mix-and-match nostalgia acts as a roadblock. There’s no attempt to consider why Wade finds these specific objects appealing, out of the billion options available to him. The book assumes up front that readers find everything in this list as unbearably cool as Cline does, and that just running down an exhaustive list of Wade’s favorite things is enough to make him appealing, relatable, and enviable. Steven Spielberg’s new film adaptation of Ready Player One prominently features that same car, but in a context that improves it immensely. Spielberg doesn’t have Wade talk audiences through it, and he doesn’t spell out the references. He just slaps the car down in the middle of a tremendous early action scene, where it’s prominent, distinctive, and memorable. Fans who want the full nostalgia trip, who want to wring every Easter egg out of the experience, will eventually be able to pause the movie and frame-by-frame through it, looking for the flux capacitor on the dashboard, checking the plates, and scanning for extra bonus material. But in the middle of the action, even to people who’ve never seen the Back to the Future movies and aren’t vibing on the connection, the car doesn’t need explaining. It’s just a sleek piece of visual energy, one breathless element among dozens of others. It’s not a citation or a list. It’s an effortless, integrated piece of the action. [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cSp1dM2Vj48] That dynamic stretches throughout Ready Player One, scripted by Cline and X-Men: The Last Stand writer Zak Penn, and directed by Spielberg as a whiplash-fast tear through a world-spanning, all-encompassing video game. The story, which mostly takes place in the virtual-reality world called The OASIS, rarely slows down enough to explain the references, or geek out over them the way the book does. It’s still a visual festival of ‘80s culture that sometimes hinges significant jokes on the assumption that the audience knows the filmography of Robert Zemeckis, or will chortle over a reference to Monty Python and the Holy Grail. But the film improves significantly on the book by prioritizing the story over the signifiers. The hardcore pop-culture crowd that is this movie’s ultimate intended audience will have plenty to pore over and pick apart in this film. But the story moves briskly enough, and with enough giant-sized, screen-friendly excitement, that it doesn’t feel like it’s aimed solely and specifically at them. Some of that speed comes at the expense of artistry. Ready Player One opens by laboriously climbing a mountain of voiceover, explaining the setting: the year is 2045, and the world is terrible. Most people live in depressing poverty, and spend as much time as possible jacked into the fantasy world of the OASIS. There, they can be and do anything they want, or at least anything they can afford to buy with coins won in the universe’s eternally running video game arenas. The OASIS was created by reclusive genius James Halliday (Bridge of Spies’ Mark Rylance), who packed it with his own favorite culture. When he died, he created a three-part quest within the world, linked to his favorite films and games, but also tied to his own past regrets and frustrations. Whoever finds the three keys he’s hidden within the game world, and the ultimate Easter egg they unlock, will get full control of OASIS and Halliday’s vast fortune. The quest has created a subclass of “egg-hunters,” or “Gunters” — quest-obsessives whose full-time occupation is hunting down the keys. It’s also created an evil dystopian megacorp, run by former Halliday intern Nolan Sorrento (Ben Mendelsohn, of Rogue One and Starred Up), and devoted to gaining control of the OASIS to commercialize it. Wade (X-Men: Apocalypse’s Tye Sheridan) and his fellow Gunters — particularly too-cool-for-school solo hunter Art3mis (Olivia Cooke, also currently starring in the chilling Thoroughbreds) and Wade’s big mechanical buddy Aech (Master of None’s Lena Waithe) — all want the keys and the egg for their own personal reasons, though those are barely articulated. Cline’s book assumes everyone will know a DeLorean is cool; Spielberg’s film assumes the same thing about a teenage protagonist who loves playing video games. Wade (or Parzival, as he’s known in the OASIS) eventually develops an ethos, but for the most part, he’s like every other video gamer who’s ever sat down on a couch and hit “start” on the controller. He may appreciate the gameplay or the storyline or the people he meets online, but ultimately, he just wants that elusive win. He’s more a customized audience avatar than a real character, but that’s fitting for a world that’s so spottily drawn, at least outside of the virtual paradise where people prefer to spent their time. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/9820163/29ed3d416cd513893ea80d1e6c9a560e.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The film version of Ready Player One has some major advantages over the book. The exposition is just as bald, but once it’s done, Spielberg can focus on the endless dynamism of a world where anything is possible. As Wade and others follow their quest through races, battles, and puzzles, they encounter a dizzying blur of visual references that act as “Hey, remember this?” in-jokes with the audience, including some major ones that weren’t in the book. But the filmmakers also delve into Halliday’s past and his wounded psyche, in a way that gradually becomes a little touching and tragic. (A conversation with Halliday’s online avatar closely recalls a similar scene with Professor Falken in WarGames, and carries the same sense of melancholy.) The film also goes further than the book in laying out why Halliday’s retreat into a fantasy world wasn’t necessarily good for anyone — especially not for Halliday himself. No matter how validating the onscreen gags are, they’re still a reminder of a man who found more emotional resonance in Jurassic Park’s T-Rex than in a connection with a living human being. The film inevitably has its cake and eats it too when it comes to addressing wish-fulfillment fantasy and delirious nostalgia: the story can only push so far in sorrowing over Halliday’s surrender and retreat from the world, while still turning every rambunctious game setpiece into a celebration of Cline’s favorite culture. Ready Player One is so heavily inspired by and inflected with the broad, black-and-white morality of ‘80s geek culture that any attempt to find the gray areas feels slightly daring, even as it feels slightly out of place. Given that Sorrento is a buttoned-down, stony-faced idea-thief of an evil overlord, straight out of Tron, there’s not a lot of room for narrative nuance in this story. But at least Cline and Penn make the effort, acknowledging some of the biggest complaints leveled at Cline’s book, and trying to take the story a little deeper. The film version does carry over some of the book’s most notable flaws, especially a suspicious reliance on narrative convenience and coincidence. The characters are thinly drawn, and most of them are little more than cool avatars and signature moves. There’s no sense that anyone involved with the story really cares about the details of the real world in this crapsack future, given how little the real-world scenes hold together. And the film takes a particularly feather-light approach to what should be significant emotions, especially when a death that should devastate Wade is shrugged off within seconds, then brought back out for a cheap, unearned moment much later. Spielberg’s signature sentiment is operating in full force, as he builds up one highly symbolic confrontation solely for the feelings of triumph and justice it creates, and then has it come to exactly nothing. And in places, the story jumps forward so quickly that it feels like necessary connective scenes are simply missing. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/10408527/ready_player_one.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Unequivocally, the film’s biggest problem is the half-assed love story between Wade and Art3mis, which operates on approximately 75 percent wish-fulfillment and 25 percent apathetic inevitability. When they first encounter each other, Wade is starstruck: he knows Art3mis from her online cool-girl rep, and watching her in action, he sees her as an über-badass with leet skillz and an appealingly punk devil-may-care attitude. It’s a short, shocking jump from there to him telling her he loves her. What follows should be important and telling — she reminds him that they don’t know each other, that he’s seeing an online avatar and a mental picture he’s largely invented. (And, of course, he thinks they’re perfect for each other because she gets his references.) But the film never follows through on that mature and useful point. The insta-relationship that develops between them is as inauthentic and insulting as the central romance in Edgar Wright’s Scott Pilgrim Vs. The World, without any of the sense of irony or intentionality. It’s bad enough to follow the “hero wins the girl as a prize” model without examining it at all. It’s worse still to have the characters examine it, find the flaws, then instantly forget about them. This isn’t a movie with a long memory (except when it’s reaching back 40 years for visual gags), but it’s infuriating to see it try to examine its own tropes responsibly, then take no steps whatsoever to address the issues it raises. And yet, when Wade is in his kitted-out DeLorean, tearing along a preposterously difficult game racetrack, menaced by King Kong and dodging flying debris as his fellow racers crash and burn, very little of that matters. The sheer dynamism and energy of the movie are compelling, even when the character drama isn’t. The action scenes are deliberately overclocked and overwhelming, turning Wade’s quest into a thrilling blur of fast-paced decisions and the endorphin-rush highs of a good gaming experience. More importantly, the film is overtly funny in ways that constantly remind the audience that there are people behind the game avatars, and specifically people who are sometimes young, self-absorbed, immature, and caught up in their own created self-images of badassery. The human frailties behind the game avatars is a reliable well of humor for Ready Player One, and the script takes full, hilarious advantage. And while the film’s real world gets left behind in the rush, the attention to detail during the OASIS scenes is absolutely astounding — not just the details Cline salivated over on the page, like that Knight Rider scanner in the grill of Wade’s car, but the subtle nuances, like the way Wade’s avatar constantly seems to be standing in a flattering breeze that ruffles his hair in the most winsome way possible, or the way Art3mis’ too-big anime eyes catch the light. The uncanny-valley effect is strong in these game avatars, but Spielberg uses it to his advantage, reminding his audience at every moment that what they’re seeing is mostly a fantasy, created by people who see image as almost everything. It’s a slick, sleek, surface fantasy, for sure. But for people who share Cline’s worldview, or identify with gamer culture in general, it’s an immense hit of validation and acknowledgement, delivered with joyful abandon and unmissable enthusiasm. All those feelings of love and obsession came through clearly on the page. But on the screen, they’re bigger and better, because they’re so much more intense, and so much closer to the memorable images that turned Cline into an obsessive in the first place. This review was initially published after Ready Player One’s premiere at the 2018 SXSW festival in Austin, Texas. The film arrives in theaters on March 29th, 2018.

articles.title: Breaking the Voodoo curse: D’Angelo, Black Messiah, and the perils of perfection
articles.summary: After 14 years of near silence, the savior of soul set the internet on fire last night
articles.body_text: I heard D’Angelo for the first time at the turn of the new millennium, and like many people, I felt that I had stumbled onto the savior of modern music. His 2000 masterpiece Voodoo was a completely unique mixture of funk, R&B, gospel, and hip-hop: the guiding star of the nascent neo-soul genre. It went to number one on the Billboard charts, sold millions of copies, and won numerous high profile awards. You could be forgiven for asking, “How is he going to top that?” The answer was brutally simple: he didn’t. For the last 14 years D’Angelo has been silent, save a few middling singles and numerous rumors about his health, sanity, and the progress of a follow up. And then, without much warning, it arrived at midnight last night, a 12-track album entitled Black Messiah. For a man whose career essentially missed the modern internet, new music from D’Angelo did not fail to set social media on fire. I feel conflicted about critiquing this record, mostly because I’m just overjoyed that D’Angelo feels comfortable and confident to make and release new music. I’m rooting for him, in other words, in a way that I don’t for most musicians. Voodoo was such a powerful antidote to the stuff that passed for R&B at my high school, hits from teeny boppers like Britney Spears, N’Sync, and 98 Degrees. If I’m being brutally honest, however, Black Messiah doesn’t measure up. The greatest joy of Voodoo was D’Angelo’s vocal range, alternating from silky smooth to ragged gospel to lascivious funk. He plays with that diversity on this new album, but to me his vocals sound far less distinctive and are often buried beneath a layer of distortion that smothers the transcendent sensation I get listening to tracks like Voodoo’s “Untitled (How Does It Feel).” On “How Does It Feel,” D’Angelo’s voice is double- and triple-layered, crafting elegant harmonies with himself. The instrumental backing is minimal, building to a series of crescendos around his aching vocals. It was a rare instance of an artist baring himself completely — both musically and, in the unforgettable video, physically. It made him into a sex symbol and, more than decade later, hasn’t lost any of its power. The video is four and half minutes, but for the real experience, listen to the full album version and wait for that moment six minutes in (Six. Minutes.) when he completely lets loose. All of which is to say, Black Messiah is music that I like. It’s full of live instrumentation, interesting arrangements, and strikingly human vocals that stand out against the majority of singers on the charts and in the clubs these days. There are weird digressions and also tight grooves, but ultimately the new D’Angelo sounds like what it is: the tortured follow-up to an album that cannot be topped, plagued by 14 years of self-doubt from the singular genius at the center of it. On “Back to the Future (Part I),” D’Angelo sings “So if you’re wondering about the shape I’m in / I hope it ain’t my abdomen you’re referring to.” That’s a sly joke about his personal struggles with substance abuse and weight gain, a nice moment where he shows a sense of humor about the demons that have kept him silent for so long. I think that’s why I feel like such a heel for reviewing this album. Every album cannot be a new Voodoo; hell, it’s possible he’ll never reach those highs again. I’m just happy D’Angelo is back, and apparently the rest of the internet is, too. I hope this record, whatever its flaws, means we can expect more new music from him, preferably sooner than 2028.

The hardcore pop-culture crowd that is this movie’s ultimate intended audience will have plenty to pore over and pick apart in this film. But the story moves briskly enough, and with enough giant-sized, screen-friendly excitement, that it doesn’t feel like it’s aimed solely and specifically at them. Some of that speed comes at the expense of artistry. Ready Player One opens by laboriously climbing a mountain of voiceover, explaining the setting: the year is 2045, and the world is terrible. Most people live in depressing poverty, and spend as much time as possible jacked into the fantasy world of the OASIS. There, they can be and do anything they want, or at least anything they can afford to buy with coins won in the universe’s eternally running video game arenas. The OASIS was created by reclusive genius James Halliday (Bridge of Spies’ Mark Rylance), who packed it with his own favorite culture. When he died, he created a three-part quest within the world, linked to his favorite films and games, but also tied to his own past regrets and frustrations. Whoever finds the three keys he’s hidden within the game world, and the ultimate Easter egg they unlock, will get full control of OASIS and Halliday’s vast fortune. The quest has created a subclass of “egg-hunters,” or “Gunters” — quest-obsessives whose full-time occupation is hunting down the keys. It’s also created an evil dystopian megacorp, run by former Halliday intern Nolan Sorrento (Ben Mendelsohn, of Rogue One and Starred Up), and devoted to gaining control of the OASIS to commercialize it. Wade (X-Men: Apocalypse’s Tye Sheridan) and his fellow Gunters — particularly too-cool-for-school solo hunter Art3mis (Olivia Cooke, also currently starring in the chilling Thoroughbreds) and Wade’s big mechanical buddy Aech (Master of None’s Lena Waithe) — all want the keys and the egg for their own personal reasons, though those are barely articulated. Cline’s book assumes everyone will know a DeLorean is cool; Spielberg’s film assumes the same thing about a teenage protagonist who loves playing video games. Wade (or Parzival, as he’s known in the OASIS) eventually develops an ethos, but for the most part, he’s like every other video gamer who’s ever sat down on a couch and hit “start” on the controller. He may appreciate the gameplay or the storyline or the people he meets online, but ultimately, he just wants that elusive win. He’s more a customized audience avatar than a real character, but that’s fitting for a world that’s so spottily drawn, at least outside of the virtual paradise where people prefer to spent their time. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/9820163/29ed3d416cd513893ea80d1e6c9a560e.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The film version of Ready Player One has some major advantages over the book. The exposition is just as bald, but once it’s done, Spielberg can focus on the endless dynamism of a world where anything is possible. As Wade and others follow their quest through races, battles, and puzzles, they encounter a dizzying blur of visual references that act as “Hey, remember this?” in-jokes with the audience, including some major ones that weren’t in the book. But the filmmakers also delve into Halliday’s past and his wounded psyche, in a way that gradually becomes a little touching and tragic. (A conversation with Halliday’s online avatar closely recalls a similar scene with Professor Falken in WarGames, and carries the same sense of melancholy.) The film also goes further than the book in laying out why Halliday’s retreat into a fantasy world wasn’t necessarily good for anyone — especially not for Halliday himself. No matter how validating the onscreen gags are, they’re still a reminder of a man who found more emotional resonance in Jurassic Park’s T-Rex than in a connection with a living human being. The film inevitably has its cake and eats it too when it comes to addressing wish-fulfillment fantasy and delirious nostalgia: the story can only push so far in sorrowing over Halliday’s surrender and retreat from the world, while still turning every rambunctious game setpiece into a celebration of Cline’s favorite culture. Ready Player One is so heavily inspired by and inflected with the broad, black-and-white morality of ‘80s geek culture that any attempt to find the gray areas feels slightly daring, even as it feels slightly out of place. Given that Sorrento is a buttoned-down, stony-faced idea-thief of an evil overlord, straight out of Tron, there’s not a lot of room for narrative nuance in this story. But at least Cline and Penn make the effort, acknowledging some of the biggest complaints leveled at Cline’s book, and trying to take the story a little deeper. The film version does carry over some of the book’s most notable flaws, especially a suspicious reliance on narrative convenience and coincidence. The characters are thinly drawn, and most of them are little more than cool avatars and signature moves. There’s no sense that anyone involved with the story really cares about the details of the real world in this crapsack future, given how little the real-world scenes hold together. And the film takes a particularly feather-light approach to what should be significant emotions, especially when a death that should devastate Wade is shrugged off within seconds, then brought back out for a cheap, unearned moment much later. Spielberg’s signature sentiment is operating in full force, as he builds up one highly symbolic confrontation solely for the feelings of triumph and justice it creates, and then has it come to exactly nothing. And in places, the story jumps forward so quickly that it feels like necessary connective scenes are simply missing. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/10408527/ready_player_one.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Unequivocally, the film’s biggest problem is the half-assed love story between Wade and Art3mis, which operates on approximately 75 percent wish-fulfillment and 25 percent apathetic inevitability. When they first encounter each other, Wade is starstruck: he knows Art3mis from her online cool-girl rep, and watching her in action, he sees her as an über-badass with leet skillz and an appealingly punk devil-may-care attitude. It’s a short, shocking jump from there to him telling her he loves her. What follows should be important and telling — she reminds him that they don’t know each other, that he’s seeing an online avatar and a mental picture he’s largely invented. (And, of course, he thinks they’re perfect for each other because she gets his references.) But the film never follows through on that mature and useful point. The insta-relationship that develops between them is as inauthentic and insulting as the central romance in Edgar Wright’s Scott Pilgrim Vs. The World, without any of the sense of irony or intentionality. It’s bad enough to follow the “hero wins the girl as a prize” model without examining it at all. It’s worse still to have the characters examine it, find the flaws, then instantly forget about them. This isn’t a movie with a long memory (except when it’s reaching back 40 years for visual gags), but it’s infuriating to see it try to examine its own tropes responsibly, then take no steps whatsoever to address the issues it raises. And yet, when Wade is in his kitted-out DeLorean, tearing along a preposterously difficult game racetrack, menaced by King Kong and dodging flying debris as his fellow racers crash and burn, very little of that matters. The sheer dynamism and energy of the movie are compelling, even when the character drama isn’t. The action scenes are deliberately overclocked and overwhelming, turning Wade’s quest into a thrilling blur of fast-paced decisions and the endorphin-rush highs of a good gaming experience. More importantly, the film is overtly funny in ways that constantly remind the audience that there are people behind the game avatars, and specifically people who are sometimes young, self-absorbed, immature, and caught up in their own created self-images of badassery. The human frailties behind the game avatars is a reliable well of humor for Ready Player One, and the script takes full, hilarious advantage. And while the film’s real world gets left behind in the rush, the attention to detail during the OASIS scenes is absolutely astounding — not just the details Cline salivated over on the page, like that Knight Rider scanner in the grill of Wade’s car, but the subtle nuances, like the way Wade’s avatar constantly seems to be standing in a flattering breeze that ruffles his hair in the most winsome way possible, or the way Art3mis’ too-big anime eyes catch the light. The uncanny-valley effect is strong in these game avatars, but Spielberg uses it to his advantage, reminding his audience at every moment that what they’re seeing is mostly a fantasy, created by people who see image as almost everything. It’s a slick, sleek, surface fantasy, for sure. But for people who share Cline’s worldview, or identify with gamer culture in general, it’s an immense hit of validation and acknowledgement, delivered with joyful abandon and unmissable enthusiasm. All those feelings of love and obsession came through clearly on the page. But on the screen, they’re bigger and better, because they’re so much more intense, and so much closer to the memorable images that turned Cline into an obsessive in the first place. This review was initially published after Ready Player One’s premiere at the 2018 SXSW festival in Austin, Texas. The film arrives in theaters on March 29th, 2018.

articles.body_text: S-ledaren Magdalena Andersson gick ut i Expressen med sitt bud till Vänsterpartiet. Men innan det vädjade Vänsterpartiet till S att inte publicera debattartikeln. ”Obegripligt”, skriver Ida Gabrielsson (V) på X om S-draget. Missa inget om regeringsbildningen – ladda ner Expressens app Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. I förra veckan publicerade S sitt totalpaket. S, MP och C i regering – V utanför men som stödparti. Från Vänsterpartiets håll har draget genererat upprörda röster. Inte bara för att V återigen hålls ute från regeringen utan även för att S valde att meddela om det gemensamma startpaketet i en debattartikel i Expressen. Vice partiledare Ida Gabrielsson skriver på X att V fick information om att S skulle skiva debattartikeln ”kort innan den skulle publicera” men är inte nöjd. ”Vi bad dom att inte göra det och i stället skicka över budet så vi kunde mötas och diskurera det. Men dom valde att köra en debattartikel i stället” skriver hon. S-toppen Mikael Damberg säger i ”P1 Morgon” att de ”naturligtvis skickat förslaget till Vänsterpartiet också” och att debattartikeln var ett ”initiativ för att få Vänstern in i förhandlingar om vägen framåt”. – Poängen är att det har spridits en bild av att samtalen vi har haft är ett nytt januariavtal, där det är extrem högerpolitik som ligger på bordet, säger Damberg.

articles.title: Familjen om sorgen efter mordet på My
articles.summary: Deras dotter mördades under julhelgen förra året. Snart väntas åtal mot mördaren. Nu tackar familjen i Rönninge för stödet de fått.
articles.body_text: Deras dotter mördades under julhelgen förra året. Snart väntas åtal mot den misstänkta mördaren. Nu tackar familjen i Rönninge för stödet de fått. ”Inför den kommande rättegången betyder ert stöd oerhört mycket för oss” , skriver familjen till TT genom ett ombud. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Natten mot annandag jul i fjol försvann 25-åriga My i Rönninge utanför Stockholm. Dagen därpå hittades hon mördad. ” Att förlora vår älskade dotter och syster är en sorg som inte går att beskriva med ord. Saknaden och smärtan finns med oss varje dag ”, skriver familjen till TT genom ett ombud. 26-åriga Vilma Andersson sitter häktad för mord och grovt gravfridsbrott. Åtalet väntas i december. ” Vi vill rikta ett varmt och innerligt tack till alla som har visat oss omtanke och stöd efter det fruktansvärda som drabbat vår familj. Inför den kommande rättegången betyder ert stöd oerhört mycket för oss ”, skriver familjen till TT. Familjen skriver vidare att de inte kommer att kommentera rättegången och vädjar till både medier och allmänheten att respektera deras sorg och integritet. Vilma Andersson har erkänt grovt gravfridsbrott, men förnekar mord. Enligt en rättspsykiatrisk undersökning led han inte av en allvarlig psykisk störning under tiden för brottet. Han har dömts för grova brott tidigare, bland annat kidnappningsförsök av en flicka.

articles.title: Gabrielsson: Det här saknar V i erbjudandet

articles.body_text: 20 minuter tog det – sen slog Vänsterpartiet ner budet från S, MP och C. På X förklarar vice partiledare Ida Gabrielsson varför. ”Nu får det vara slut på tramset”, skriver hon. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. I en debattartikel i Expressen presenterar S-ledaren Magdalena Andersson ett erbjudande för Vänsterpartiet . Hon skriver att Socialdemokraterna, Centerpartiet och Miljöpartiet har förhandlat fram ”ett startpaket med politiska reformer” som man garanterar V. Artikeln publicerades klockan 17.53 på söndagen. Exakt 20 minuter senare kom ett svar från Vänsterpartiets vice partiledare Ida Gabrielsson på X: ”Tack men nej tack! Det är vare sig konstruktivt eller förtroendeingivande att förhandla via debattartiklar.” Gabrielsson har varit en flitig twittrare under regeringsförhandlingarna, och i ytterligare ett inlägg under kvällen förklarar hon närmare varför S, C:s och MP:s förslag skjuts ner. Enligt henne framställs ”budet” som att ”V ska låta övriga regera på våra mandat” – och hon saknar flera frågor. ”Marknadsskolan, a-kassan och karensen är inte ens med, inte heller en ordentlig indexering av välfärden. Och C sa nej till dessa reformer i dom samtal där regeringsfrågan diskuterades”, skriver Gabrielsson.

articles.body_text: Lars-Johan Åge är expert på förhandling, har jobbat för FBI och för polisens insatsstyrka. Ida Gabrielsson, Vänsterpartiets vice ordförande, reagerar starkt. ”Vi har uttryckligen bett om att inte skicka in en debattartikel utan gå direkt till oss,” skriver hon på X. – Nu har vi ju hållit de här förhandlingarna och samtalen väldigt internt.
